absences.what: An ancient text this project holds an antecedent of and does not carry onto this element, and no rightsholder has refused any of it. No witness this project holds prints the Latin of the postconciliar Missal itself; that book is in copyright and is not held here. What IS held is the facing-column Latin of the 1861 Philadelphia Cummiskey hand missal, public domain and transcribed in six tracked artifacts, and ten elements of this file now carry it. These four do not, and each is refused for a reason about itself rather than about anyone's permission. The Kyrie: the witness sets the Greek acclamations as three rows of three, the ninefold form, and this Missal prints six, two to each invocation, a simplification this repository's study names in terms; joining the witness's rows would print nine acclamations under an element of six, and dropping three of them to fit would be an editorial act performed on a witness, which is as much a fabrication as normalising its spelling. The prayer for peace: the study quotes the 2002 Latin entire and its endnote states the prayer is retained from the older Roman Order - and the two strings are still not the same strings. The witness reads ne respicias peccata MEA where the quoted text reads peccata NOSTRA, and the witness carries a conclusion, qui vivis et regnas Deus per omnia saecula saeculorum Amen, that the quoted text does not. Publishing on the strength of the word retained would have put the wrong pronoun into the Rite of Peace on every day of this calendar. The priest's private preparation: the same study names the second of the two prayers Perceptio Corporis et Sanguinis tui and the witness prints Perceptio corporis tui, which does not name the Blood. The alternative Agnus Dei: that element exists only because the ecumenical English witness prints two ENGLISH forms of one invocation, while the Missal prints one Latin text of it, which the element above already carries; giving this one Latin as well would print one Latin text twice under two keys and assert a Latin variant the Missal does not have. The Kyrie becomes reachable when the element or the witness's arrangement is modelled honestly. The two divergent prayers are not reachable from this witness at all, and no older book can supply what they need, because the difference at each is the Missal's own. The alternative Agnus Dei is settled and correct as it stands.

This element models the whole Roman Canon as one span, nn. 83-98, Te igitur through Per ipsum with the institution narrative inside it, and that is why nothing can be sourced onto it. The obstacle is the model and not the rights: this repository's study calls the Roman Canon the only one of the four Eucharistic Prayers not composed or assembled in the twentieth century, and the 1861 witness sets it in twenty-one public-domain rows. But the two Canons were established Latin against Latin from hash-verified facsimiles of both books and differ at eleven places, among them both consecratory forms, and every one of those places falls inside this element's extent. Carrying the older Canon here would print the reform's changes as though they were not there. The element must first be split into the received sub-prayers the older book already sets separately - Te igitur, Memento Domine, Communicantes, Hanc igitur, Quam oblationem, Qui pridie, Unde et memores, Supra quae, Supplices, Memento etiam, Nobis quoque, Per quem, Per ipsum - after which the places the reform changed are isolated and the rest are reachable. That split is a larger change than this file, and until it is made this element stays empty.

The reform's own new matter, and this is the class for which the rights refusal is the true reason. The Latin of the postconciliar Missal is a work of the Holy See, first published in 1969, revised in 1975 and 2002, with the emended reprint of 2008; it is a post-1929 foreign work, protected in the United States, and this project has established no distribution basis for it. For these twelve elements no public-domain antecedent establishes the wording either, so nothing may be carried from an older book instead. This repository's tracked study of this Order of Mass states, at the loci its endnotes give, that the two Penitential Act forms II and III are new compositions in their present arrangement; that the two Benedictus es prayers over the bread and the chalice are new compositions which replaced the medieval offertory prayers Suscipe sancte Pater and Offerimus tibi Domine; that Prayers II, III and IV are twentieth-century compositions, Prayer II being an adaptation which does not print the ancient anaphora it is built on; and that the acclamation after the consecration is wholly new. Four more are recastings of ancient matter, where the older prayer is public domain and is NOT this element's text: the mingling formula is a shortened form of a Roman Christmas collect and the older witness carries an opening clause and a full conclusion the Missal deleted; the washing of hands prints a shortened verse of a different psalm from the one the older Order recited; the invitation to Communion is the older Ecce Agnus Dei joined to the beatitude of Revelation 19:9, which the study places among the substantially changed; and the two-word Communion formula with the communicant's Amen replaces the longer formula the older Order gave the priest alone. What is refused is the Missal's own composed or recast wording. Nothing here refuses the ancient prayers underneath the recastings, which are public domain and are not what these elements print.

The element models a span of the Missal wider than any one prayer, and the span contains matter this repository's own study places on both sides of its retained-and-changed line, so no witness can be joined to the element as it stands. This is a modelling fact about this file and not a refusal by anyone. Element by element: the Greeting carries four forms, of which the 1861 holds one; the first Penitential Act carries an invitation the witness does not have at all, and its Confiteor is printed there only as Confiteor Deo omnipotenti &c. with the transcriber's own note that the full prayer is not obtainable from it, its other form being the ministers' prayer addressed to the priest; the Gospel dialogue announces Lectio sancti Evangelii where the witness announces Sequentia vel initium, and the witness has no Verbum Domini after the Gospel; the embolism at n. 125 carries with it the people's doxology Quia tuum est regnum, which the study calls ancient in the Greek East and never part of the Roman Mass, a genuine importation, and the witness's own embolism differs in extent at both ends; the Pax carries n. 127, whose versicle and response the witness holds verbatim, together with n. 128 Offerte vobis pacem, for which it holds nothing; the Blessing carries three regimes - simple, solemn or prayer over the people, and the pontifical form - of which the witness supplies none in Latin; and the Dismissal carries the ancient Ite missa est with its answer together with the three formulas the 2008 reprint added, while the witness's own alternative is Benedicamus Domino, which is none of the three. Split any of these at the Missal's own numbering and its ancient half becomes sourceable at once; until then there is no honest single sourcing.

The approved English of the Roman Missal is the International Commission on English in the Liturgy's, (c) ICEL 2010, and is published here with acknowledgement under ICEL's own standing Global Computer Networks permission for the elements whose text ICEL's own free chant library and the England-and-Wales Liturgy Office print. This absence covers the elements that are still empty in English for reasons other than ICEL's permission: the Eucharistic Prayers, the Confiteor and the Apostles' Creed, whose text the England-and-Wales leaflets carry but which are not yet spliced onto tracked TSV payloads; the ecumenical-text elements that carry the ELLC text rather than the Missal's; and the not-a-text elements that carry no words at all. What was written here before -- that this project holds no exact copy of the words -- was true when it was written and is no longer true. The copies exist, they are registered, and twenty-three elements of the invariant frame carry them.

An ancient text for which this project holds no Latin witness at all, which is the witness's silence and not a rights question. The Apostles' Creed is not an element of the Tridentine or 1962 Order of Mass, so neither the 1861 Cummiskey nor the 1862 Pustet Ordo prints it, and a search of this repository finds it in no book, in no language column; locating a public-domain Latin witness of the Roman baptismal symbol is a clean acquisition task nobody has opened. The fraction and commingling formula is printed by the 1861 inside an English rubric set across the full measure, with no facing Latin - the same class the 1962 file records as no-facing-latin - and this repository's study places that formula on its retained list, so the text is ancient and the gap is a page nobody here has read. The 1862 Pustet would print it, but that artifact is uncorrected OCR whose own record says to quote from it only through a checked passage, and no passage record stands over it.

These twelve elements carry no words of their own at this layer, so nothing is withheld and nothing is missing; the key exists because calling their emptiness a rights refusal would turn a modelling fact into a claim that the rite omits something. Eight are frame markers for an action or a chant - the entrance and the veneration of the altar, the first and second readings, the responsorial psalm, the Alleluia or Lenten acclamation, the homily, the universal prayer whose n. 20 is one line and no formulary, and the veneration and departure - and six of the twelve carry no Latin incipit at all. Four are propers of the day, whose text belongs to the propers layer and not to this invariant frame: the Collect, the Prayer over the Offerings, the Preface, and the Prayer after Communion. The Prefaces are the one row here with mixed matter underneath: the constitution's own two categories are taken from the more ancient tradition of the Roman Church or newly composed, the two must not be conflated in either direction, and whoever opens that corpus must classify prayer by prayer rather than treat it as one thing.

A prayer the Priest says quietly, for which this project holds no exemplar, and nobody has refused anything. Six elements are empty for this reason: the mingling of water and wine at n. 24, In spiritu humilitatis at n. 26, the washing of hands at n. 28, the commingling formula at n. 129, the Priest's two prayers of private preparation at n. 131, and the purification at n. 137; two more are empty only in part, the prayers over the bread and the chalice at nn. 23 and 25, whose people's acclamation is carried and whose prayers are not, and the Communion at nn. 133-136, whose formula at the distribution is carried and whose two formulas at the Priest's own Communion are not. The gap is a consequence of how the rite is celebrated and of what a publisher therefore publishes. ICEL's free library is a library of CHANTS, and these prayers are never sung, so it has no page for any of them. The Bishops' Conference leaflets are participation aids, and these prayers are not the people's, so they print a rubric where the prayer stands. So no free official publisher has reason to print them and none does. What would close it is one exemplar of the whole Order of Mass rather than of its sung or its people's parts: the Missal's own study edition, an ICEL reference copy of the Order of Mass, or any authoritative complete printing this project can open and hash. Until one is registered these elements stay empty, and the reason is a page nobody here has read and not a permission nobody has given.

advisory: A finding aid for the shape of the rite, and never a book to celebrate from. Most of this Order of Mass is missing here, and every element says which of its two texts is missing and why, because they are not missing for one reason. The English side has two reasons now. The approved English is the International Commission on English in the Liturgy's, (c) ICEL 2010, and it IS published here with acknowledgement under ICEL's own standing Global Computer Networks permission: twenty-three elements of the invariant frame carry it, drawn from ICEL's own free chant library (Music for the Roman Missal) and from the Liturgy Office of the Catholic Bishops' Conference of England and Wales, every word read on a fetched and hash-verified page. The elements still empty in English are empty for a different reason, recorded here as `priest-prayer-said-quietly`: prayers the Priest says quietly, for which no free official publisher prints a page, because they are never sung and are not the people's parts. The Latin side has six reasons, and they run from the reform's own new matter, which is the Holy See's and is withheld, to a rubric that has no words in any book. Where a text is missing what stands in its place is the element's received Latin incipit, which is a reference and not the prayer. THE LATIN THAT IS HERE IS NOT THIS MISSAL'S. Ten elements carry Latin, and at every one of them it is the facing column of an 1861 Philadelphia lay hand missal printing the ancient prayer this Order of Mass received. The Latin of the editio typica itself is in copyright and is not held by this project, in any element, anywhere on this page. Each of the ten says beside its own words which prayer of that older book it is, at which printed page and leaf, which accidents of that printing it carries unnormalised, and whether its identity with the controlling edition has been established by a collation this repository holds or is so far only asserted. Four are established; six are not, and they say so. A few elements still carry the ecumenical text of the English Language Liturgical Consultation, which the rightsholder grants freely and which is NOT what is said at Mass in the dioceses of the United States. Where the ecumenical text and the Missal's own differ a reader will see it at once: the ecumenical text answers the greeting "And also with you" and opens the Creed "We believe in one God", where the 2011 Roman Missal has "And with your spirit" and "I believe in one God".
derived_from: The order, the numbering, the Latin incipits, the speakers and the conditions are transcribed from this repository's own collated study of the Order of Mass, src/claude/liturgy/roman-rite/postconciliar/2008-latin-2011-us-english/ordinary/00-order-of-mass, and in particular its research/sequence-inventory.md, which gives one row per received boundary in the Missal's own order and numbering against the 2008 editio typica tertia emendata. That study's own scope record states the boundary this file inherits: the Latin is quoted there where an argument requires it, as evidence and not as text for recitation, and the approved English is not reproduced. The English texts here are drawn from the artifact registered at artifact.english-language-liturgical-consultation.praying-together.1998.common-texts-en. The Latin texts here are drawn from a DIFFERENT BOOK, and that is the whole of what has to be understood about them: the six ordinarium, praefationes and canon-missae `-la` artifacts of edition.eugene-cummiskey.roman-missal-english-laity.philadelphia-1861, which transcribe the facing Latin column of an 1861 Philadelphia lay hand missal from a registered scan at 640 dpi, one physical line per printed block, each row carrying its own printed page, Internet Archive leaf and transcriber's note. Those artifacts are already the Latin of this project's 1962 frame; here they are joined to a second calendar, element by element, because the older book prints the ancient prayer the postconciliar Missal received and for no other reason. Nothing is transcribed afresh for this file and nothing is normalised: the join names artifact rows that already exist and already carry their hash.
edition: Missale Romanum, editio typica tertia 2008, reimpressio emendata 2008

elements.name: Entrance and veneration of the altar
elements.note: The entrance chant, the procession, the veneration of the altar, and the sign of the cross said by priest and people together.

translations.text:
All make the Sign of the Cross as the Priest says:
In the name of the Father, and of the Son,
and of the Holy Spirit.
Amen.

elements.name: The Greeting
elements.note: Three forms; a bishop greets Pax vobis. The people's answer, Et cum spiritu tuo, is the text the 2011 English changed to 'And with your spirit'; the ecumenical text served elsewhere on this page renders the same Latin 'And also with you', and the two must not be confused.
elements.speaker: all

translations.text:
The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ,
and the love of God,
and the communion of the Holy Spirit
be with you all.
Or:
Grace to you and peace from God our Father
and the Lord Jesus Christ.
Or:
The Lord be with you.
In this first greeting, a Bishop, in place of The Lord be with you, says:
Peace be with you.
And with your spirit.

elements.name: Penitential Act, form I
elements.note: The Confiteor said by all together, with the striking of the breast, and the priest's absolution. Form I of three; the celebrant chooses.
elements.speaker: all

translations.text:
Brethren (brothers and sisters), let us acknowledge our sins,
and so prepare ourselves to celebrate the sacred mysteries.
A brief pause for silence follows.
Have mercy on us, O Lord.
For we have sinned against you.
Show us, O Lord, your mercy.
And grant us your salvation.
The absolution by the Priest follows:
May almighty God have mercy on us,
forgive us our sins,
and bring us to everlasting life.
Amen.

elements.latin_incipit: Qui missus es sanare contritos corde
elements.name: Penitential Act, form III
elements.note: Tropes set before the Kyrie acclamations. Where this form is used the Kyrie that follows is not repeated.
elements.speaker: all

translations.text:
Brethren (brothers and sisters), let us acknowledge our sins,
and so prepare ourselves to celebrate the sacred mysteries.
There follows a brief pause for silence. The Priest, or a Deacon or another minister, then says the following or other invocations with Kyrie, eleison (Lord, have mercy):
You were sent to heal the contrite of heart:
Lord, have mercy. Or: Kyrie, eleison.
Lord, have mercy. Or: Kyrie, eleison.
You came to call sinners:
Christ, have mercy. Or: Christe, eleison.
Christ, have mercy. Or: Christe, eleison.
You are seated at the right hand of the Father to intercede for us:
Lord, have mercy. Or: Kyrie, eleison.
Lord, have mercy. Or: Kyrie, eleison.
The absolution by the Priest follows:
May almighty God have mercy on us,
forgive us our sins,
and bring us to everlasting life.
Amen.

elements.name: Kyrie eleison
elements.note: The Missal prints the Kyrie in Greek and in the sixfold form, two acclamations to each invocation, and omits it where the third form of the Penitential Act has been used. The ecumenical text below gives the Greek and an English rendering of it; the Missal's own English is ICEL's and is not here.
elements.speaker: all

translations.text:
The Kyrie eleison (Lord, have mercy) invocations follow, unless they have just occurred in a formula of the Penitential Act.
Lord, have mercy.
Lord, have mercy.
Christ, have mercy.
Christ, have mercy.
Lord, have mercy.
Lord, have mercy.
Or:
Kyrie, eleison.
Kyrie, eleison.
Christe, eleison.
Christe, eleison.
Kyrie, eleison.
Kyrie, eleison.

elements.name: Gloria in excelsis
elements.note: Said on Sundays outside Advent and Lent, on solemnities and feasts, and on more solemn celebrations.
elements.speaker: all

translations.text:
Glory to God in the highest,
and on earth peace to people of good will.
We praise you,
we bless you,
we adore you,
we glorify you,
we give you thanks for your great glory,
Lord God, heavenly King,
O God, almighty Father.
Lord Jesus Christ, Only Begotten Son,
Lord God, Lamb of God, Son of the Father,
you take away the sins of the world,
have mercy on us;
you take away the sins of the world,
receive our prayer;
you are seated at the right hand of the Father,
have mercy on us.
For you alone are the Holy One,
you alone are the Lord,
you alone are the Most High,
Jesus Christ,
with the Holy Spirit,
in the glory of God the Father.
Amen.

translations.note: ANTECEDENT, NOT THE CONTROLLING EDITION. The Latin here is the facing column of the 1861 Philadelphia Cummiskey hand missal at its Gloria in excelsis, printed page xix, Internet Archive leaf 29, the hymn complete in one block. The Latin of the Missale Romanum, editio typica tertia 2002 with its emended reprint of 2008, is under copyright and is not held by this project; these are the 1861 printing's words and not that book's. Carried as printed and normalised nowhere: the book opens with a two-line drop G followed by LORIA in capitals, given here as GLORIA; it reads bonae voluntatis and Rex coelestis with the ae- and oe-ligatures, Jesu Christe with a J twice, and sets the closing Amen in italic. COLLATED, and on a finding rather than on a comparison of two strings, which is a weaker footing than the three elements that carry both. The cited study's endnote to n. 8 states in terms that the Latin text at n. 8 is unchanged from the older Roman form, and the study's own account of its method states that both books were read directly for that comparison. It quotes no 2002 Latin at this element, so no word-level comparison could be made here and none is claimed.
translations.text: GLORIA in excelsis Deo, et in terra pax hominibus bonæ voluntatis. Laudamus te; benedicimus te; adoramus te; glorificamus te. Gratias agimus tibi propter magnam gloriam tuam, Domine Deus, Rex cœlestis, Deus Pater omnipotens. Domine Fili unigenite Jesu Christe. Domine Deus, Agnus Dei, Filius Patris, qui tollis peccata mundi, miserere nobis. Qui tollis peccata mundi, suscipe deprecationem nostram. Qui sedes ad dexteram Patris, miserere nobis. Quoniam tu solus sanctus. Tu solus Dominus. Tu solus altissimus, Jesu Christe, cum Sancto Spiritu, in gloria Dei Patris. Amen.

elements.name: The Collect
elements.note: Proper to the day; its Latin stands in this project's propers layer, and its approved English does not.
elements.speaker: priest

elements.name: The First Reading
elements.note: The reading itself is the Lectionary's and is proper to the day; this layer carries only the frame.

translations.text:
To indicate the end of the reading, the reader acclaims:
The word of the Lord.
Thanks be to God.

elements.name: The Second Reading
elements.note: On Sundays, solemnities and feasts.

translations.text:
To indicate the end of the reading, the reader acclaims:
The word of the Lord.
Thanks be to God.

The Lord be with you.
And with your spirit.
A reading from the holy Gospel according to N.
Glory to you, O Lord.
At the end of the Gospel, the Deacon, or the Priest, acclaims:
The Gospel of the Lord.
Praise to you, Lord Jesus Christ.

elements.name: The Nicene Creed
elements.note: Said on Sundays and solemnities, with a bow prescribed at et homo factus est. The ecumenical text below opens 'We believe' and brackets 'and the Son', both of which the Roman Missal's English does not; it is the same Creed and not the same translation.
elements.speaker: all

translations.text:
I believe in one God,
the Father almighty,
maker of heaven and earth,
of all things visible and invisible.
I believe in one Lord Jesus Christ,
the Only Begotten Son of God,
born of the Father before all ages.
God from God, Light from Light,
true God from true God,
begotten, not made, consubstantial with the Father;
through him all things were made.
For us men and for our salvation
he came down from heaven,
At the words that follow, up to and including and became man, all bow.
and by the Holy Spirit was incarnate of the Virgin Mary,
and became man.
For our sake he was crucified under Pontius Pilate,
he suffered death and was buried,
and rose again on the third day
in accordance with the Scriptures.
He ascended into heaven
and is seated at the right hand of the Father.
He will come again in glory
to judge the living and the dead
and his kingdom will have no end.
I believe in the Holy Spirit, the Lord, the giver of life,
who proceeds from the Father and the Son,
who with the Father and the Son is adored and glorified,
who has spoken through the prophets.
I believe in one, holy, catholic and apostolic Church.
I confess one Baptism for the forgiveness of sins
and I look forward to the resurrection of the dead
and the life of the world to come. Amen.

translations.note: ANTECEDENT, NOT THE CONTROLLING EDITION. The Latin here is the facing column of the 1861 Philadelphia Cummiskey hand missal at its Credo, printed pages xxi-xxii, Internet Archive leaves 31-32, joined from that book's own three blocks. The Latin of the Missale Romanum, editio typica tertia 2002 with its emended reprint of 2008, is under copyright and is not held by this project; these are the 1861 printing's words and not that book's. Carried as printed and normalised nowhere: a two-line drop C followed by REDO in capitals, given here as CREDO; the ae- and oe-ligatures at terrae, coeli, coelis, saecula, saeculi; Jesum Christum and judicare with a J; ET HOMO FACTUS EST set in full capitals with the book's own asterisk keying a footnote at the foot of xxii; and Et EXPECTO, not exspecto, the word standing whole and unbroken on its own line. The second block runs over the page break, breaking at ex Maria Vir- / gine, and heavy inking at the head of xxii fills the s and e of sepultus, which the transcriber read from the surviving strokes and did not repair from any other book. The printing carries the Filioque, qui ex Patre Filioque procedit. UNCOLLATED: the identity of this text with the controlling edition's is not established here. This repository's study of this Order of Mass treats n. 18 at 00-order-of-mass/sections/30-creed-and-universal-prayer.tex:16-24 and names the Nicene Creed among the texts retained with little or no change of wording at :90-synthesis.tex:47-55, on a comparison for which it states that both books were read directly. It quotes no 2002 Latin of the symbol, so no word-level comparison has been made. The two Latin texts are conventionally taken to be identical and that convention has not been checked here.
translations.text:
CREDO in unum Deum Patrem omnipotentem, factorem cœli et terræ, visibilium omnium et invisibilium.
Et in unum Dominum Jesum Christum, Filium Dei unigenitum, et ex Patre natum ante omnia sæcula. Deum de Deo: Lumen de Lumine; Deum verum de Deo vero; genitum non factum; consubstantialem Patri, per quem omnia facta sunt. Qui propter nos homines, et propter nostram salutem descendit de cœlis. Et incarnatus est de Spiritu Sancto, ex Maria Virgine: ET HOMO FACTUS EST*. Crucifixus etiam pro nobis sub Pontio Pilato, passus et sepultus est. Et resurrexit tertia die secundum Scripturas. Et ascendit in cœlum, sedet ad dexteram Patris. Et iterum venturus est cum gloria judicare vivos et mortuos; cujus regni non erit finis.
Et in Spiritum Sanctum, Dominum et vivificantem, qui ex Patre Filioque procedit: qui cum Patre et Filio simul adoratur, et conglorificatur; qui locutus est per prophetas. Et unam sanctam Catholicam et Apostolicam Ecclesiam. Confiteor unum Baptisma in remissionem peccatorum. Et expecto resurrectionem mortuorum, et vitam venturi sæculi. Amen.

elements.name: The Apostles' Creed
elements.note: May be used in place of the Nicene Creed, especially in Lent and Eastertide. The 2008 emended reprint corrected its opening from Credo in unum Deum to Credo in Deum.
elements.speaker: all

translations.text:
I believe in God, the Father almighty,
creator of heaven and earth.
I believe in Jesus Christ, God's only Son, our Lord,
who was conceived by the Holy Spirit,
born of the Virgin Mary,
suffered under Pontius Pilate,
was crucified, died, and was buried;
he descended to the dead.
On the third day he rose again;
he ascended into heaven,
he is seated at the right hand of the Father,
and he will come to judge the living and the dead.
I believe in the Holy Spirit,
the holy catholic Church,
the communion of saints,
the forgiveness of sins,
the resurrection of the body,
and the life everlasting. Amen.

elements.name: The Universal Prayer
elements.note: The intentions are composed locally and no book carries them.

sections.name: The Creed and the Universal Prayer

elements.latin_incipit: Per huius aquae et vini mysterium
elements.name: The mingling
elements.speaker: priest

translations.note: ANTECEDENT, NOT THE CONTROLLING EDITION. The Latin here is the facing column of the 1861 Philadelphia Cummiskey hand missal at its In spiritu humilitatis, printed page xxiv, Internet Archive leaf 34. The Latin of the Missale Romanum, editio typica tertia 2002 with its emended reprint of 2008, is under copyright and is not held by this project; these are the 1861 printing's words and not that book's. THE WITNESS MISPRINTS nodie FOR hodie, and it is carried as printed and not corrected: the letter is an n, with no ascender, read at 200 per cent magnification against the h of hoc on the same page and recorded in the artifact's own transcriber's note. It is that printer's error. Nothing here attributes it to the Missal, and correcting it silently would have manufactured a witness to a book nobody opened. UNCOLLATED: the identity of this text with the controlling edition's is not established here. This repository's study of this Order of Mass states at n. 26, in 00-order-of-mass/sections/40-preparation-of-the-gifts.tex:108-110, that the prayer is taken from the Song of the Three Young Men and is retained from the older Order, and it quotes the 2002 Latin of the opening clause only, as far as suscipiamur a te, Domine. That clause and this witness agree word for word. The rest of the prayer, the misprint among it, has not been compared with anything.
translations.text: In spiritu humilitatis, et in animo contrito suscipiamur a te, Domine: et sic fiat sacrificium nostrum in conspectu tuo nodie, ut placeat tibi, Domine Deus.

elements.latin_incipit: Lava me, Domine, ab iniquitate mea
elements.name: The washing of hands
elements.speaker: priest

translations.text:
Pray, brethren (brothers and sisters),
that my sacrifice and yours
may be acceptable to God,
the almighty Father.
May the Lord accept the sacrifice at your hands
for the praise and glory of his name,
for our good
and the good of all his holy Church.

translations.note: ANTECEDENT, NOT THE CONTROLLING EDITION. The Latin here is the facing column of the 1861 Philadelphia Cummiskey hand missal at its Orate fratres and Suscipiat Dominus, printed page xxvii, Internet Archive leaf 37, joined from the book's own two blocks. The Latin of the Missale Romanum, editio typica tertia 2002 with its emended reprint of 2008, is under copyright and is not held by this project; these are the 1861 printing's words and not that book's. Carried as printed and normalised nowhere: Fratres is capitalised and patrem is not, as the book sets them; the Latin column points a comma after nominis sui where its own facing English points none; there is a comma after nostram; Ecclesiae suae sanctae carries the ae-ligature throughout; and the response's R. mark is the book's, which prefixes the answer in both columns and prefixes the summons in neither. COLLATED. The cited study quotes the 2002 Latin of both texts at n. 29 and its endnote states that both are retained from the older Roman Order without material change; setting that quotation beside these two rows, they agree word for word, the only differences being the capitalisation, the pointing and the ligatures named above.
translations.text:
Orate Fratres: ut meum ac vestrum sacrificium acceptabile fiat apud Deum patrem omnipotentem.
R. Suscipiat Dominus sacrificium de manibus tuis ad laudem et gloriam nominis sui, ad utilitatem quoque nostram, totiusque Ecclesiæ suæ sanctæ.

elements.name: The Prayer over the Offerings
elements.note: Proper to the day.
elements.speaker: priest

elements.name: The dialogue before the Preface
elements.note: The ecumenical text below answers the greeting 'And also with you' and the assent 'It is right to give our thanks and praise'; the Roman Missal's English has 'And with your spirit' and 'It is right and just'.
elements.speaker: all

translations.text:
The Lord be with you.
And with your spirit.
Lift up your hearts.
We lift them up to the Lord.
Let us give thanks to the Lord our God.
It is right and just.

translations.note: ANTECEDENT, NOT THE CONTROLLING EDITION. The Latin here is the facing column of the 1861 Philadelphia Cummiskey hand missal at its Preface dialogue, printed page xxvii, Internet Archive leaf 37, where the whole dialogue stands as one continuous block in each column with the P. and R. run in, and is the last block on that page. The Latin of the Missale Romanum, editio typica tertia 2002 with its emended reprint of 2008, is under copyright and is not held by this project; these are the 1861 printing's words and not that book's. Carried as printed and normalised nowhere: the book reads Dignum et JUSTUM est, which is its own j-for-i convention and not a variant reading, and its P. and R. marks are its own setting of a dialogue the Missal sets the same way. COLLATED. The cited study quotes the 2002 Latin of the whole dialogue at n. 31, calling it the oldest continuously attested dialogue in the Latin liturgy; set beside this row the two agree word for word, the sole divergence being justum for iustum.
translations.text: P. Dominus vobiscum. R. Et cum spiritu tuo. P. Sursum corda. R. Habemus ad Dominum. P. Gratias agamus Domino Deo nostro. R. Dignum et justum est.

elements.name: The Preface
elements.note: Fifty Prefaces, proper to the day, the season, or the Eucharistic Prayer itself. They are not carried in this layer.
elements.speaker: priest

elements.latin_incipit: Sanctus, Sanctus, Sanctus Dominus Deus Sabaoth
elements.name: Sanctus and Benedictus
elements.speaker: all

translations.text:
Holy, Holy, Holy Lord God of hosts.
Heaven and earth are full of your glory.
Hosanna in the highest.
Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.
Hosanna in the highest.

translations.note: ANTECEDENT, NOT THE CONTROLLING EDITION. The Latin here is the facing column of the 1861 Philadelphia Cummiskey hand missal at its Sanctus, printed page xxviii, Internet Archive leaf 38, where that book sets the Sanctus once only, after the Prefaces. The Latin of the Missale Romanum, editio typica tertia 2002 with its emended reprint of 2008, is under copyright and is not held by this project; these are the 1861 printing's words and not that book's. Carried as printed and normalised nowhere: the book capitalises only the first Sanctus of the three, reads coeli with the oe-ligature, and prints no cross glyph before Benedictus in this column. UNCOLLATED: the identity of this text with the controlling edition's is not established here. This repository's study of this Order of Mass names the Sanctus among the texts retained with little or no change of wording, at 00-order-of-mass/sections/90-synthesis.tex:47-55, on a comparison for which it states that both books were read directly. It quotes no 2002 Latin at this element, so no word-level comparison has been made; and that same retention list is known to mislead, since at two elements of this file it says retained where the words are not in fact the same words.
translations.text: Sanctus, sanctus, sanctus, Dominus Deus Sabaoth. Pleni sunt cœli et terra gloria tua. Hosanna in excelsis. Benedictus qui venit in nomine Domini, Hosanna in excelsis.

elements.name: Eucharistic Prayer I, the Roman Canon
elements.note: Te igitur, Memento Domine, Communicantes, Hanc igitur, Quam oblationem, Qui pridie, the Mysterium fidei and the people's acclamation, Unde et memores, Supra quae, Supplices, Memento etiam, Nobis quoque, Per quem haec omnia, Per ipsum. THIS IS NOT THE CANON OF THE 1962 MISSAL, and the English Canon this site serves under that missal is not a translation of this prayer. Established Latin against Latin from hash-verified facsimiles of both books, they differ at eleven places, among them both consecratory forms: this prayer adds quod pro vobis tradetur over the bread, DELETES mysterium fidei from the form over the chalice, replaces Haec quotiescumque feceritis with Hoc facite in meam commemorationem, and adds a Mysterium fidei acclamation the older book has nowhere. The 1962 book prints nineteen signs of the cross over the pages compared; this prayer prints one.
elements.speaker: priest

elements.latin_incipit: Vere Sanctus es, Domine, fons omnis sanctitatis
elements.name: Eucharistic Prayer II
elements.note: With a preface of its own, which may be replaced. Its shape is drawn from the anaphora of the so-called Apostolic Tradition; the drafting history is not established here.
elements.speaker: priest

elements.latin_incipit: Vere Sanctus es, Domine, et merito te laudat
elements.name: Eucharistic Prayer III
elements.note: Has no preface of its own and takes the day's. A formula for the dead stands at n. 115.
elements.speaker: priest

elements.name: Eucharistic Prayer IV
elements.note: Its preface is fixed and may not be replaced, so it is excluded whenever a proper Preface is appointed.
elements.speaker: priest

elements.name: The acclamation after the consecration
elements.note: Three alternative acclamations. This element has no counterpart in the 1962 Missal, where mysterium fidei stands inside the form over the chalice instead.
elements.speaker: all

translations.text:
The mystery of faith.
We proclaim your Death, O Lord,
and profess your Resurrection
until you come again.
Or:
When we eat this Bread and drink this Cup,
we proclaim your Death, O Lord,
until you come again.
Or:
Save us, Savior of the world,
for by your Cross and Resurrection
you have set us free.

elements.latin_incipit: Per ipsum, et cum ipso, et in ipso
elements.name: The final doxology
elements.note: The people's Amen closes it. Here per omnia saecula saeculorum is part of the doxology itself; in the 1962 book it follows as a separate versicle of priest and minister.
elements.speaker: priest

translations.text:
He takes the chalice and the paten with the host and, raising both, he says:
Through him, and with him, and in him,
O God, almighty Father,
in the unity of the Holy Spirit,
all glory and honor is yours,
for ever and ever.
Amen.

translations.note: ANTECEDENT, NOT THE CONTROLLING EDITION. The Latin here is the facing column of the 1861 Philadelphia Cummiskey hand missal at its Per ipsum and the versicle that closes its Canon, printed pages xxxviii-xxxix, Internet Archive leaves 48-49, joined from that book's own two blocks. The Latin of the Missale Romanum, editio typica tertia 2002 with its emended reprint of 2008, is under copyright and is not held by this project; these are the 1861 printing's words and not that book's. Carried as printed and normalised nowhere: the book prints no cross signs in this block, which the older Roman rite marks five times; it reads saecula saeculorum with the ae-ligature, set unbroken here where the same versicle at the foot of xxvii prints a full stop after saecula; and it sets the Amen in italic. THE SHAPE DIFFERS AND THE MARKS SHOW IT: the witness's P. and R. divide the closing versicle between priest and minister, which is the older Order, where this Missal makes per omnia saecula saeculorum the end of the doxology itself and the people's Amen answers the whole. The marks are the witness's and are not this Missal's rubric. UNCOLLATED: the identity of this text with the controlling edition's is not established here. This repository's study of this Order of Mass records at 00-order-of-mass/sections/55-roman-canon.tex:114 that the prayer text is substantially identical from Te igitur to Per ipsum apart from the changes to the dominical words, which fall elsewhere in the Canon and not in this element. It quotes no 2002 Latin of the doxology, so no word-level comparison has been made.
translations.text:
Per ipsum, et cum ipso, et in ipso, est tibi Deo Patri omnipotenti, in unitate Spiritus Sancti, omnis honor et gloria.
P. Per omnia sæcula sæculorum. R. Amen.

elements.name: The Lord's Prayer
elements.note: The ecumenical text is given whole, as the Consultation prints it, which is how its licence requires it to be reproduced. The Roman Rite does not say it continuously: the last two lines are the doxology Quia tuum est regnum, and the embolism Libera nos stands between them and the rest.
elements.speaker: all

translations.text:
After the chalice and paten have been set down, the Priest, with hands joined, sings:
At the Savior's command
and formed by divine teaching,
we dare to say:
He extends his hands and, together with the people, continues:
Our Father, who art in heaven,
hallowed be thy name;
thy kingdom come,
thy will be done
on earth as it is in heaven.
Give us this day our daily bread,
and forgive us our trespasses,
as we forgive those who trespass against us;
and lead us not into temptation,
but deliver us from evil.

translations.note: ANTECEDENT, NOT THE CONTROLLING EDITION. The Latin here is the facing column of the 1861 Philadelphia Cummiskey hand missal at its Praeceptis salutaribus and Pater noster, printed page xxxix, Internet Archive leaf 49, joined from that book's own two blocks. The Latin of the Missale Romanum, editio typica tertia 2002 with its emended reprint of 2008, is under copyright and is not held by this project; these are the 1861 printing's words and not that book's. Carried as printed and normalised nowhere: the invitation opens with a two-line drop P followed by Raeceptis, a capital R and the rest lower-case, with the ae-ligature, given here as printed; the prayer reads coelis and coelo with the oe-ligature and quotidianum for cotidianum; and the book runs the response R. Sed libera nos a malo and the priest's italic P. Amen. into the same block, which is the older Order's division of the prayer between priest and ministers and not this Missal's. UNCOLLATED: the identity of this text with the controlling edition's is not established here. This repository's study of this Order of Mass quotes the 2002 Latin of the INVITATION at n. 124, in 00-order-of-mass/sections/70-communion-rite.tex:19-23, and that quotation and this witness's first row agree word for word. It quotes no 2002 Latin of the Our Father itself, which is the larger half of this element and has been compared with nothing. The study names the Pater noster with its introduction among the texts retained with little or no change of wording, and records the change that is real: the people now say it with the priest, where in the older Roman Order the priest said it and the ministers answered the last petition.
translations.text:
PRæceptis salutaribus moniti, et divina institutione formati, audemus dicere:
Pater noster, qui es in cœlis, sanctificetur nomen tuum: adveniat regnum tuum: fiat voluntas tua sicut in cœlo, et in terra: panem nostrum quotidianum da nobis hodie; et dimitte nobis debita nostra, sicut et nos dimittimus debitoribus nostris: et ne nos inducas in tentationem: R. Sed libera nos a malo. P. Amen.

elements.latin_incipit: Libera nos, quaesumus, Domine, ab omnibus malis
elements.name: The embolism
elements.speaker: priest

translations.text:
With hands extended, the Priest alone continues, singing:
Deliver us, Lord, we pray, from every evil,
graciously grant peace in our days,
that, by the help of your mercy,
we may be always free from sin
and safe from all distress,
as we await the blessed hope
and the coming of our Savior, Jesus Christ.
He joins his hands.
The people conclude the prayer, acclaiming:
For the kingdom,
the power and the glory are yours
now and for ever.

elements.latin_incipit: Domine Iesu Christe, qui dixisti Apostolis tuis
elements.name: The prayer for peace
elements.speaker: priest

translations.text:
Then the Priest, with hands extended, sings aloud:
Lord Jesus Christ,
who said to your Apostles:
Peace I leave you, my peace I give you,
look not on our sins,
but on the faith of your Church,
and graciously grant her peace and unity
in accordance with your will.
He joins his hands.
Who live and reign for ever and ever.
Amen.

elements.name: The Pax and the sign of peace
elements.note: The exchange itself is pro opportunitate.
elements.speaker: all

translations.text:
The peace of the Lord be with you always.
And with your spirit.
Then, if appropriate, the Deacon, or the Priest, adds:
Let us offer each other the sign of peace.
And all offer one another a sign, in keeping with local customs, that expresses peace, communion, and charity. The Priest gives the sign of peace to a Deacon or minister.

elements.latin_incipit: Agnus Dei, qui tollis peccata mundi
elements.name: Agnus Dei
elements.note: The Consultation's own form, which names Jesus and unfolds tollis in two ways. Repeatable as long as the fraction lasts.
elements.speaker: all

translations.text:
Lamb of God, you take away the sins of the world,
have mercy on us.
Lamb of God, you take away the sins of the world,
have mercy on us.
Lamb of God, you take away the sins of the world,
grant us peace.
The invocation may even be repeated several times if the fraction is prolonged. Only the final time, however, is grant us peace said.

translations.note: ANTECEDENT, NOT THE CONTROLLING EDITION. The Latin here is the facing column of the 1861 Philadelphia Cummiskey hand missal at its Agnus Dei, printed page xl, Internet Archive leaf 50. The Latin of the Missale Romanum, editio typica tertia 2002 with its emended reprint of 2008, is under copyright and is not held by this project; these are the 1861 printing's words and not that book's. Carried as printed and normalised nowhere: the book does not write the invocation out three times. It sets three asterisks at the head of three short lines, * miserere nobis, twice and then * dona nobis pacem., the asterisk marking where Agnus Dei, qui tollis peccata mundi is resumed, and they are run in here as the sibling English row runs them. A reader must expand them as the book intends and not read four clauses where the rite has three invocations. UNCOLLATED: the identity of this text with the controlling edition's is not established here. This repository's study of this Order of Mass describes n. 130 at 00-order-of-mass/sections/70-communion-rite.tex:86-91 and names the Agnus Dei among the texts retained with little or no change of wording, on a comparison for which it states that both books were read directly; it quotes the 2002 Latin of the ending dona nobis pacem only, which this witness matches. The invocation itself has been compared with nothing.
translations.text: Agnus Dei, qui tollis peccata mundi, * miserere nobis, * miserere nobis, * dona nobis pacem.

elements.latin_incipit: Agnus Dei, qui tollis peccata mundi
elements.name: Agnus Dei, the alternative form
elements.note: The more traditional of the two forms the Consultation prints. Both are given because the choice between them is the reader's and not this project's.
elements.speaker: all

translations.text:
Lamb of God, you take away the sin of the world,
have mercy on us.
Lamb of God, you take away the sin of the world,
have mercy on us.
Lamb of God, you take away the sin of the world,
grant us peace.

elements.latin_incipit: Domine Iesu Christe, Fili Dei vivi
elements.name: The priest's private preparation
elements.note: Two forms; the priest chooses one and says it inaudibly.
elements.speaker: priest

elements.name: The invitation to Communion
elements.note: The people answer Domine, non sum dignus, once, with the priest.
elements.speaker: all

translations.text:
The Priest genuflects, takes the host and, holding it slightly raised above the paten or above the chalice, while facing the people, sings aloud:
Behold the Lamb of God,
behold him who takes away the sins of the world.
Blessed are those called to the supper of the Lamb.
And together with the people he adds once:
Lord, I am not worthy
that you should enter under my roof,
but only say the word
and my soul shall be healed.

translations.note: ANTECEDENT, NOT THE CONTROLLING EDITION. The Latin here is the facing column of the 1861 Philadelphia Cummiskey hand missal at its Quod ore sumpsimus, printed pages xlii-xliii, Internet Archive leaves 52-53, the block running over the page break at fiat nobis re- / medium. The Latin of the Missale Romanum, editio typica tertia 2002 with its emended reprint of 2008, is under copyright and is not held by this project; these are the 1861 printing's words and not that book's. Carried as printed and normalised nowhere: the book points a comma after temporali which the study's quotation of the 2002 text does not. COLLATED. The cited study quotes the 2002 Latin of this prayer entire at n. 137 and calls it a post-Communion prayer of great antiquity, retained; set beside this row the two agree word for word, the sole divergence being that comma.
translations.text: Quod ore sumpsimus, Domine, pura mente capiamus, et de munere temporali, fiat nobis remedium sempiternum.

elements.name: The Prayer after Communion
elements.note: Proper to the day.
elements.speaker: priest

elements.name: The Blessing
elements.note: A simple blessing; or a solemn blessing or prayer over the people, introduced by Inclinate vos ad benedictionem; or, for a bishop, the pontifical form with Sit nomen Domini benedictum and Adiutorium nostrum.
elements.speaker: priest

translations.text:
Then the dismissal takes place. The Priest, facing the people and extending his hands, sings:
The Lord be with you.
And with your spirit.
The Priest blesses the people, singing:
May almighty God bless you,
the Father, and the Son, ✠ and the Holy Spirit.
Amen.
In a Pontifical Mass, the Celebrant receives the miter and, extending his hands, sings:
The Lord be with you.
And with your spirit.
Blessed be the name of the Lord.
Now and for ever.
Our help is in the name of the Lord.
Who made heaven and earth.
The Celebrant receives the pastoral staff, if he uses it, and sings:
May almighty God bless you,
Making the Sign of the Cross over the people three times, he adds:
the Father, ✠ and the Son, ✠ and the Holy ✠ Spirit.
Amen.
The Deacon or, in his absence, the Priest himself, sings the invitation:
Bow down for the blessing.

elements.name: The Dismissal
elements.note: The 2008 emended reprint added three alternative formulas to Ite, missa est.
elements.speaker: all

translations.text:
Then the Deacon, or the Priest himself, with hands joined and facing the people, sings:
Go forth, the Mass is ended.
Thanks be to God.
Or:
Go and announce the Gospel of the Lord.
Thanks be to God.
Or:
Go in peace, glorifying the Lord by your life.
Thanks be to God.
Or:
Go in peace.
Thanks be to God.
The following dismissal is used on Easter Sunday, the Octave of Easter, and in the Mass during the Day on Pentecost Sunday.
Go forth, the Mass is ended, alleluia, alleluia.
Or:
Go in peace, alleluia, alleluia.
Thanks be to God, alleluia, alleluia.

elements.name: The veneration of the altar and departure
elements.note: Omitted where another liturgical action follows immediately.

slots_derived_from: Where each proper of the day stands inside this frame is read from the same collated study as the order of the elements, and each slot's locus is the Missal's own numbering of the element it is anchored to. No facsimile of the editio typica is held here, so unlike the 1962 frame these placements rest on that study and on the Missal's numbering rather than on pages this project has opened; the numbering is nonetheless the Missal's own statement of the order, and every slot below anchors to an element whose number this file already carries.
title: The Order of Mass

This library predates the 2013 insertion of Saint Joseph into Eucharistic Prayers II-IV and the collect conclusions emended after the Prefect's letter of May 2020; neither emendation touches any text carried from it here, and that has been checked element by element rather than assumed. This is not an approved altar Missal, it carries no concordat cum originali, and it is neither sponsored nor endorsed by ICEL.
translations.label: The approved English of the Roman Missal, from ICEL's own free chant library (Music for the Roman Missal, web state of 21 August 2026)

translations.acknowledgement: English translations of the Kyrie eleison, Gloria in Excelsis, the Nicene Creed, the Apostles' Creed, the Sursum Corda, the Sanctus and Benedictus, the Agnus Dei and the Lord's Prayer, © 1998, English Language Liturgical Consultation (ELLC), and used by permission. www.englishtexts.org
translations.caution: NOT the approved English of the Roman Missal, which is ICEL's and is under copyright. This is the ecumenical text agreed among English-speaking churches, and it differs from the Missal's English in wording a reader will notice. It is offered here because its rightsholder grants free use in terms, and for no other reason. Nothing here may be used for recitation.
translations.label: Praying Together, the ecumenical common texts (English Language Liturgical Consultation, 1998)

translations.caution: NOT the Latin of the Missale Romanum. The postconciliar Missal's Latin is a work of the Holy See, is under copyright, and is not held by this project; nothing served under this witness is that book's text and no element here claims to be. What is here is the facing Latin column of an 1861 Philadelphia lay hand missal - never an altar book, never an approved liturgical translation, and pre-1955 in its rubrics and its discipline - which prints the ancient prayers this Order of Mass received. It is joined element by element, and only where an element's Latin is that ancient prayer; where the reform composed, recast or rearranged, nothing is carried and the element says why. Its orthography and its misprints are its own and are carried as printed: justum for iustum, Jesu for Iesu, Et expecto for Et exspecto, the ae- and oe-ligatures, and nodie for hodie at In spiritu humilitatis are the 1861 printer's and not the Holy See's. Every element carrying Latin states beside its own words which prayer of that book it is, at which printed page and Internet Archive leaf, which accidents it carries, and whether its identity with the controlling edition has been established or is so far only asserted. Nothing here may be used for recitation.
translations.label: Antecedent Latin (NOT the Missale Romanum's text): the facing Latin column of The Roman Missal translated into the English language for the use of the laity, first revised edition (Philadelphia: Eugene Cummiskey, 1861)

variants.name: Eucharistic Prayer
variants.what: The postconciliar Missal prints four Eucharistic Prayers and the priest chooses among them; the first may always be used, and the Missal states where the fourth may not. The 1962 Missal has one Canon and no such choice, so this control belongs to this missal alone. The option marked default here is the first the Missal itself prints. That is the only order this project can state without preferring one prayer over another, and it is not a recommendation.
